candidates.topic: The Hiroo Onoda — Soldier Who Fought for 29 Years After WWII Ended
candidates.teaser: A Japanese soldier kept fighting in the jungle for nearly three decades — because no one told him the war was over.
candidates.video_title: He Fought a War That Ended 29 Years Ago
candidates.video_description: Hiroo Onoda was a Japanese soldier who continued fighting in the Philippine jungle until 1974, refusing to believe World War II had ended in 1945. He only stopped when his former commanding officer flew in personally to relieve him of duty.
candidates.script: In 1974, a soldier emerged from a Philippine jungle — armed, loyal, and ready to fight. The problem? World War II had ended 29 years earlier. Hiroo Onoda never surrendered because no one gave him the order. He ambushed patrols, avoided capture, and dismissed leaflets announcing Japan's defeat as enemy propaganda. It took his original commanding officer flying from Japan to personally stand before him and say: the war is over. He was 52 years old. Would you have believed it?

candidates.topic: The Smell of Space — Astronauts Describe It
candidates.teaser: Astronauts who've been to open space agree it has a very specific smell — and it's nothing like you'd expect.
candidates.video_title: Space Actually Has a Smell — Astronauts Agree
candidates.video_description: Multiple astronauts have reported that space has a distinct, consistent odor after spacewalks — described as seared steak, hot metal, and welding fumes. Scientists believe it's caused by high-energy particles reacting with equipment or possibly dying stars.
candidates.script: Every astronaut who's done a spacewalk reports the exact same thing: space has a smell. Not nothing. Not clean air. They describe it as seared steak, hot metal, and welding fumes all at once. It clings to their suits the moment they come back inside. Scientists believe it's caused by dying stars releasing high-energy particles that react with equipment — essentially, you're smelling stellar death. So the universe isn't silent and odorless. What else have we been wrong about?

candidates.topic: The Vantablack — The Color That Erases Depth Perception
candidates.teaser: There's a substance so dark that your brain physically cannot process the shape of whatever it covers.
candidates.video_title: This Color Makes Your Brain Stop Working
candidates.video_description: Vantablack, developed in 2014, absorbs 99.965% of all light that hits it, making any 3D object coated in it look like a flat black hole. Your visual cortex relies on reflected light to judge depth and shape — Vantablack provides none, causing genuine perceptual failure.
candidates.script: Coat a crumpled ball of tinfoil in Vantablack and it looks like someone cut a perfect circle out of reality. No shadows. No edges. No depth. Just nothing. Developed in 2014, it absorbs 99.965% of all light — your brain gets zero reflected information, so it stops rendering the shape entirely. Sculptures coated in it look like flat silhouettes. Your visual cortex isn't broken — it's just never encountered something that gives it absolutely nothing to work with. What does that say about how much of reality we actually see?

candidates.topic: The Mimic Octopus — One Animal That Impersonates Dozens
candidates.teaser: There's an octopus that doesn't just hide — it actively pretends to be completely different animals on demand.
candidates.video_title: This Animal Can Become Any Other Animal
candidates.video_description: The mimic octopus, discovered in 1998 off Indonesia, can impersonate at least 15 different species — including lionfish, flatfish, and sea snakes — adjusting its body shape, color, and movement in real time based on which local predator its attacker fears most.
candidates.script: This octopus doesn't just change color — it decides which animal to become based on who's threatening it. Spotted by a predator that fears lionfish? It flattens its arms into spines and impersonates one. Threatened near a burrow? It coils into a banded sea snake. The mimic octopus, discovered in 1998 off Indonesia, can convincingly imitate at least 15 different species in real time. It's not instinct — researchers believe it's a deliberate choice. So is this the smartest animal in the ocean?

candidates.topic: The Celsius-Fahrenheit Inventor Disagreement — The Scale Was Upside Down
candidates.teaser: The temperature scale used by billions of people was originally invented completely backwards — freezing was 100 and boiling was zero.
candidates.video_title: Celsius Invented His Scale Completely Backwards
candidates.video_description: Anders Celsius originally defined his scale in 1742 with 0° as boiling and 100° as freezing — the exact opposite of what we use today. It was reversed after his death by fellow scientists who found the inverted system counterintuitive, yet kept his name on it.
candidates.script: When Anders Celsius invented his temperature scale in 1742, boiling water was zero and freezing was 100. Completely upside down. He genuinely thought counting down to boiling made more logical sense. After he died in 1744, other scientists quietly flipped the entire scale — but kept his name. So every time you read a weather forecast in Celsius, you're using a scale its inventor would find backwards. The man had no idea what we did to his life's work. Does that bother you, or does it even matter?
